name: Quadriceps femoris
func: The four-part muscle on the front of the thigh. It straightens the knee for standing, walking, kicking and jumping, and steadies the kneecap. One part also helps lift the thigh.

levels.kid:
The **quadriceps** is the big muscle on the **front of your thigh**. "Quad" means four, because it is really **four muscles** working together as a team.

All four join onto your **kneecap** and then onto your shinbone. When they squeeze, they **straighten your knee**.

You use your quads to stand up, walk, kick a ball, jump and climb stairs. They also help you **land softly** when you jump down, so your knees do not buckle. They are some of the strongest muscles in your body!
levels.hs:
The **quadriceps femoris** is the large muscle group on the **front (anterior compartment)** of the thigh. It has four parts:

**Rectus femoris**: the straight middle muscle on top. It is the only one that starts on the hip bone (the **anterior inferior iliac spine** and just above the hip socket), so it crosses both the hip and knee.
**Vastus lateralis**: the largest, on the outer side of the thigh.
**Vastus medialis**: on the inner side, forming a teardrop bulge above the knee.
**Vastus intermedius**: deep, under rectus femoris, lying on the femur.

The three vasti start on the **femur**. All four join into the **quadriceps tendon**, which wraps around the **patella** and continues as the **patellar ligament** to the **tibial tuberosity**.

The quadriceps is the main **extensor of the knee**. Rectus femoris also **flexes the hip**, as when kicking a ball.

It is supplied by the **femoral nerve** (L2–L4). Tapping the patellar ligament gives the **knee-jerk reflex**. Beside it, **sartorius** crosses the front of the thigh diagonally, and the hamstrings lie behind, on the back of the femur.
levels.college:
**Attachments:** rectus femoris has a **straight head** from the anterior inferior iliac spine and a **reflected head** from the ilium just above the acetabulum. Vastus lateralis arises from the greater trochanter and the lateral lip of the **linea aspera**; vastus medialis from the intertrochanteric line and the medial lip of the linea aspera; vastus intermedius from the anterior and lateral femoral shaft. A small deep muscle, **articularis genus**, pulls the suprapatellar bursa up during extension.

**Insertion:** through the quadriceps tendon onto the patella and, via the patellar ligament, the tibial tuberosity. Medial and lateral **patellar retinacula** from the vasti also insert on the tibial condyles, so some extension is possible even with a patellar fracture if the retinacula survive.

**Innervation:** the **femoral nerve (L2–L4)**, the largest branch of the lumbar plexus, which enters the thigh under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery, in the **femoral triangle**, and divides into muscular branches. It gives the **saphenous nerve**, which runs with the femoral vessels through the **adductor (subsartorial) canal** deep to sartorius.

**Blood supply:** the **lateral circumflex femoral artery** (from the profunda femoris) is the main supply, plus the femoral artery.

**Two-joint mechanics:** rectus femoris is weakest at the knee when the hip is flexed (it is slack) and strongest when the hip is extended, so a kick combines hip flexion and knee extension efficiently. Because it crosses two joints it is the most commonly strained quadriceps muscle.

**Vastus medialis obliquus (VMO):** the lowest fibres run almost horizontally and resist lateral displacement of the patella.
levels.phd:
The quadriceps is a model for studying force sharing, fatigue and atrophy. Vastus lateralis is the most-sampled muscle in human biopsy research because of its size and accessibility; untrained adults typically have roughly 40–60% type I fibres, with wide individual variation. Endurance and resistance training shift its gene expression in characteristic ways, increasing **PGC-1α**-driven mitochondrial biogenesis and **mTORC1**-driven protein synthesis, respectively.

**Arthrogenic muscle inhibition** is a key concept: after knee injury or surgery, joint swelling and damaged joint receptors reflexly inhibit quadriceps activation through spinal pathways (including Ib and flexor reflex afferent circuits and altered presynaptic inhibition), so patients cannot fully activate the muscle even if it is intact. This contributes to rapid **quadriceps atrophy** after ACL injury, and research tests interventions such as cryotherapy and neuromuscular electrical stimulation to reverse it.

The **knee-jerk reflex** is the textbook monosynaptic reflex: Ia afferents from quadriceps spindles synapse directly onto alpha motor neurons at L2–L4, with disynaptic reciprocal inhibition of the hamstrings.

The rectus femoris tendon is complex: its direct and reflected heads merge into a deep, central **intramuscular aponeurosis**, creating a "muscle within a muscle". Injuries at this central tendon heal more slowly than peripheral strains, a finding from MRI follow-up studies of athletes.

Age-related declines in quadriceps strength (**sarcopenia**) are strong predictors of falls and loss of independence; loss of type II fibre size and motor unit number contribute, and quadriceps strength is used as a functional biomarker.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** inspect for wasting, especially of the vastus medialis (an early sign after knee injury). Test knee extension against resistance and the ability to do a **straight-leg raise** (failure suggests a broken extensor mechanism). Check the **knee-jerk reflex (L3–L4 mainly)**.

**Quadriceps tendon rupture** usually affects people over 40 with predisposing conditions (kidney disease, diabetes, long-term corticosteroid treatment); a gap is felt above the patella and the patella sits low. **Patellar ligament rupture** affects younger people and the patella rides high. Both need early surgical repair. Ultrasound or MRI confirms.

**Femoral nerve lesions** (from pelvic surgery, retroperitoneal haematoma or hip surgery) cause weak knee extension, a buckling knee, an absent knee jerk and numbness of the front of the thigh and medial leg (saphenous nerve). Hip adduction is preserved, which distinguishes it from an **L3–L4 radiculopathy**, where the adductors (obturator nerve) are also weak.

**Diabetic amyotrophy** (lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy) presents with painful, asymmetric thigh wasting.

**Quadriceps contusion** ("dead leg") in contact sports can lead to **myositis ossificans**, bone forming within the muscle; avoid aggressive massage early. **Rectus femoris strains** occur in kicking and sprinting.

**Inclusion body myositis** characteristically weakens the quadriceps and finger flexors in older adults. In muscular dystrophies, the **Gowers sign** (pushing on the thighs to stand up) reflects proximal weakness of hip and knee extensors.

Rehabilitation after knee surgery focuses on regaining quadriceps activation, since weakness predicts poorer outcomes.

keyPoints: Four parts: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius
All insert via the patella and patellar ligament on the tibial tuberosity
Main knee extensor; rectus femoris also flexes the hip
Femoral nerve L2–L4; knee jerk mainly L3–L4
Straight-leg raise tests the extensor mechanism

test.q: Which quadriceps muscle also crosses the hip joint?
test.explain: Rectus femoris starts on the anterior inferior iliac spine, so it also flexes the hip.
The femoral nerve (L2–L4) enters the thigh through the femoral triangle.

test.q: What is the largest part of the quadriceps?
test.explain: Vastus lateralis on the outer thigh is the largest component.

test.q: A patient cannot do a straight-leg raise after a fall onto the knee. What does this suggest?
test.explain: Inability to keep the knee straight while lifting the leg means the quadriceps–patella–tibia chain is broken.

test.q: The teardrop-shaped bulge above the inner knee is the vastus ______.
test.explain: Its low oblique fibres (VMO) help keep the patella tracking centrally.
